opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting open questions right now. If you look at these models, they clearly have something that looks like reasoning. You can ask them a question and they'll walk through steps, and often they get it right. But it's a bit fuzzy. They'll make a small mistake in the middle of a chain, or they'll be very confident about something that doesn't quite follow, and they don't really notice.

Part of how I think about it goes back to my time working on games, on AlphaStar and following the AlphaGo line of work. There, you had a very clean signal: you win or you lose. You could combine a learned model, something like intuition, with search and planning, and the search would sharpen that intuition into something much more precise. Language models today are mostly the intuition part. They've imitated a huge amount of human text, so they have a good prior over what reasonable thinking looks like, but they haven't been pushed hard to be exactly right.

So a few things seem important to me. One is giving the model room to think: letting it spend more computation at inference time, generate multiple attempts, check its own work, backtrack. Simply allowing it to "think longer" turns out to matter a lot. The second is having some form of verification. In domains like math or code, you can check whether the answer is correct or whether the program runs and passes tests. Once you have that signal, you can do reinforcement learning on top of the pre-trained model, rewarding chains of reasoning that actually lead to correct outcomes, and that's what turns fuzzy reasoning into crisp reasoning.

The harder part is everything outside those nicely verifiable domains. Most of what we care about doesn't come with a clean reward. So a big research question is how to get good enough evaluators, whether that's models judging models, tools, or human feedback, so the reasoning can be reliable even when there's no unit test or proof checker at the end. I'm optimistic, but I'd say we're still early in figuring out how to generalize that beyond math and code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to notice is that these models already have a lot of the ingredients. If you look at what comes out of pretraining, the model has seen an enormous amount of reasoning in text: proofs, derivations, arguments, code with explanations. So the capability is latent. What it lacks is a sort of discipline around when to use it and how to verify it.

The way I think about it, there are maybe three pieces. The first is giving the model room to think. Chain of thought was the obvious version of this, but the more interesting version is treating the intermediate steps as something you can actually optimize, not just a prompting trick. If the model is allowed to spend compute at inference time, to explore, to backtrack, to say "wait, that doesn't look right," then you move from pattern-matching an answer to actually searching for one. And search is where crispness comes from, because you get to compare alternatives rather than committing to the first plausible-sounding token sequence.

The second piece is a signal for what counts as correct. This is where I think things get really interesting. In domains like math or code, you have verifiers. You can run the program, you can check the proof. So you can do reinforcement learning against that signal, and the model learns not just to produce reasoning-shaped text but reasoning that actually lands on the right answer. That's a very different training regime from imitation. With imitation, you're learning to sound like a human reasoning. With RL against a verifier, you're learning to be right, and sometimes the process that gets you there doesn't look very human at all, which is fine.

The hard part, of course, is that most of the world doesn't come with a verifier. So the third piece is figuring out how to extend that to fuzzier domains. There I think you lean on things like self-consistency, having the model critique its own outputs, using one model to check another. None of those are as clean as running a unit test, but they get you some of the way, and I suspect the capabilities you build in the verifiable domains transfer more than people expect. If a model learns to be careful in math, some of that carefulness shows up when it's reasoning about a business problem.

And then I'd add one more thing, which is calibration. Crisp reasoning isn't only about getting the right answer, it's about knowing when you don't have it. A model that says "I'm not sure, here are the two possibilities and here's what would distinguish them" is reasoning more accurately than one that confidently picks wrong. So part of this is training the models to represent their own uncertainty honestly rather than always filling in a fluent answer.

So, short version: let the model think, give it something real to check against, and teach it to know the difference between a guess and an answer. I think we're still early on all three, but the trajectory is pretty clear.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the challenge is that being able to produce a good reasoning step is different from reliably choosing the right step and knowing when you’ve made a mistake. A language model can generate something that sounds very plausible, but plausibility isn’t the same as correctness.

One way to close that gap is to give the model a way to check its work. In programming, for example, you can propose a solution, run it, look at the errors, and try again. That gives you a much stronger signal than just asking whether the explanation sounds convincing. Mathematics has some of that property as well, when you can verify the result.

Then there’s the question of how much computation you spend before answering. You could explore several approaches, compare them, and revise. But generating more text doesn’t automatically give you better reasoning. You need a useful signal for deciding which paths to pursue and which to abandon.

So I’d think about it as a combination of learning from feedback and spending computation effectively at inference time. The goal is to make checking and correcting an answer as much a part of the capability as generating it in the first place.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one important distinction is between producing an answer that sounds plausible and having a process that can actually check the answer. A language model may already contain many of the ingredients for solving a problem, but it doesn’t necessarily use them reliably on the first attempt.

So one direction is to give it more computation at inference time: let it explore a few possibilities, critique them, and revise. But more thinking alone isn’t sufficient. You need a signal that tells you whether you’re making progress. In mathematics or programming, you can sometimes verify the result, and that gives you a very useful training signal.

Then reinforcement learning can help turn that ability to occasionally find a solution into a policy that finds it consistently. The interesting question is how far we can generalize that to problems where checking the answer is itself difficult. I don’t think there’s a single trick. It’s a combination of learning better reasoning strategies, allocating computation appropriately, and knowing when you haven’t established the answer yet.
